idiom_name: object-safe trait consumed as &dyn Trait / Box<dyn Trait>
implementation_notes: A Rust trait declares the contract and cannot hold data - traits have no fields, so the stateless contract is the only shape a trait can take - while dyn Trait boxes a value and dispatches through a vtable, which is what to use when implementors are chosen at run time or mixed in one collection. The classic base-class split is replaced entirely: no inheritance, implementations are separate impl Trait for Type blocks (possibly in another crate, within the orphan rules), and the trait may supply default method bodies. Keep the trait object for dynamic collections and plugin registries; a generic bound lets the compiler see the concrete type and removes the indirection.
pitfalls: Not every trait can be a dyn trait: generic methods, Self-returning methods and async fn make it dyn-incompatible, and the error appears at the use site rather than the definition.
A trait object erases the concrete type, so inherent methods and the type's name are unavailable; recovering them needs downcasting through Any.
The orphan rule stops a contract from being implemented for foreign types outside the crate that defines the trait, so library authors must anticipate extension points up front.

variants.name: Generic trait bound / impl Trait (static dispatch)
variants.implementation_notes: A trait bound - fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T) or fn notify(item: &impl Summary) - makes the same trait a compile-time contract: the requirement is checked during type checking and the function is monomorphised, so calls are static and inlinable. This is the type-class-style realization (bounded polymorphism) rather than an interface object, and the right default for library APIs, where callers get precise diagnostics and no allocation; remember that each instantiation is a distinct function, and that a collection of mixed implementors still needs Box<dyn Trait>.
pitfalls: Monomorphisation duplicates code per implementing type, so heavy blanket bounds push compile time and binary size into every caller.
impl Trait in return position hides the concrete type: callers cannot name it or call inherent methods, and the function cannot return either of two different implementors.
Bounds do not erase: two implementations are two unrelated types, so a Vec<T> with a bound cannot hold mixed implementors.
